title: The older brother (Luke 15:25–32)
hookLine: the faithful son won't come to the party; the story ends with the father pleading
last: WHILE HE WAS STILL FAR OFF.

lines: A FINE PLACE TO ROLL THE CREDITS.
cards: Robe, ring, the fatted calf. A fine place to roll the credits. But the story began with a certain man who had two sons.
While the party starts, the older one is still out in the field, working, as he has for years. He comes near the house and hears music. Dancing.
He calls a servant over and asks what on earth is going on.

teach.b: Your brother is home, the servant says, and your father has killed the fatted calf. In the King James Bible: "And he was angry, and would not go in: therefore came out his father, and intreated him."
The father went out to the younger son on the road. Now he goes out again, to the older one in the yard, leaving his own party to plead.

And the older son lets it all out: "Lo, these many years do I serve thee, neither transgressed I at any time thy commandment: and yet thou never gavest me a kid, that I might make merry with my friends."
Not even a young goat. The word for serve is the word for working as a slave. He's been home all along, living like a hired hand.
And he names his brother: this thy son. Not my brother. The father answers gently, with a tender word, teknon, child: "Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine."
Everything was already his. He never had to earn it.
Then the father hands the brother back to him: "It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found."

teach.h: THIS THY SON, THIS THY BROTHER.
THE STORY STOPS AT THE DOOR.
teach.b: And the story stops. We never find out if he goes in. Jesus leaves the door open and the music playing.

teach.h: SON, THOU ART EVER WITH ME.
teach.b: He was talking to people grumbling that he ate with sinners, and some readers hear them in the older brother. Others hear anyone who has been faithful a long time and quietly started keeping score.

how: Christians often reflect on both brothers when reading this parable in Lent, and some preachers point to the open ending as a question each listener answers in their own life.

games.q: you're the older son. you've worked all day, and you come home to music: your wasteful brother is back and there's a feast. what do you do?
o: go straight in and join the dancing.
stand outside, angry, and refuse to go in.
games.why: "he was angry, and would not go in: therefore came out his father, and intreated him." and the story stops before we learn his answer.

practice: Think of a celebration you'd rather skip, because someone is being welcomed who, in your view, hasn't earned it: a colleague's promotion, a sibling's second chance.

Notice the old scorecard come out, then hear the father's words to his older son: all that I have is thine. If you pray, hold those words a while; if not, imagine walking in through the door, toward the music.

wordCard.voice: Teknon, Greek for child: the tender name the father gives his older, faithful son, who wouldn't come to the party.

orig.note: Greek: child. the tender word the father uses for his angry older son.
